design.decidesAndAsks:
The approach is fixed by confirmed sources. Apple's Shortcuts guide confirms POST with a JSON body; the INNOQ post confirms the Bearer header in Get Contents of URL; Apple's Siri page confirms a shortcut runs by saying its name; the open-source ChatGPT-Siri shortcut confirms the dictate, call, speak pattern with follow-up turns. In the repo, an agent key already works from the internet at the agent door.

Asked once, at build time:
- Whether voice is wanted now (contract section 13).
- Whether the phone key may change things or only look.

Sparkie and the door decide alone:
- Which conversation the words belong to (30-minute rolling).
- The wait (8 s by default; the Shortcut may send `wait` from 2 to 40).
- The answer length, and when to say "the rest is in the chat".
- Reading "spark three" as Spark 3.
- Lookups always run without asking.

Sparkie asks first, in one spoken question:
- Any change by voice except remembering: the console speaks its own label from the real plan ("Stop sc-gemma on Spark 3? Say yes or no."). Only a plain "yes" within 15 minutes runs it; "no" puts it away.
- A name that fits several models or none: it names the options and the owner answers in words, which pass the same gate as typed words (sparkieCheck).
- Empty or garbled dictation: "I didn't catch that."

It does not ask, it redirects:
- A change on a look-only key: it says the key can only look.
- A question only the owner may answer (stopping something started outside Spark Console, or the model that answers Sparkie): "That one needs you in Spark Console."

Limits found in the code:
- Multi-step requests by voice do the first step only, because carrying on is off for key conversations (14-chats.mjs:342).
- Sparkie's speed on tool answers is not measured, so many answers may pass 8 s and take the "still working" path.
guardRails: Look-only by default. Letting the phone key change things is the existing second step with the owner's passkey (24-handler.mjs:261, 22-passkey.mjs:118).
The phone key is its own entry in Access, Agents, removable alone, and works only at /say: not the agent door's tools, not the model address (/v1). An ordinary agent key may also use /say.

Only the key's SHA-256 hash is kept on Spark 2 (agents.json, owner-only file); the key is shown once. The owner's password is never involved. On the phone the key sits in the Shortcut, which iCloud syncs to the owner's devices. Do not share the Shortcut by link; if it is ever shared, put an import question on the header field, which Apple clears on sharing.

By voice no change runs on the first sentence. The spoken question is the console's own label built from the real plan, not the model's wording, and only a plain yes within 15 minutes runs exactly that. Pending questions are lost on a restart, so a late yes does nothing. Remembering is the one exception: the line is said back and can be forgotten.
Questions only the owner may answer cannot be answered by voice; they need the page (runChoice, 14-chats.mjs:87).

Existing rails unchanged: 12 changes an hour then an automatic pause, the pause switch, never Sparkie's model, Spark 2 or protected containers, 8 GB kept free, and an audit line per call with the key's name and the words.
Never SSH, Tailscale, firewall, users or keys. No Funnel or port change: it rides the existing :8443. With Funnel off it works only with Tailscale on the phone.
No notifications: the door speaks only when asked. Operation results wait in the conversation and are read on the next ask.

Dictated words are the words of whoever holds the key, with that key's rights and nothing more. Tool results, logs and web text stay data. `say` goes through the existing secret masking, and ids and addresses are stripped.

Lock screen: Apple says Siri asks to unlock only for shortcuts that open an app, and this one opens none, so assume it can run locked. That is why look-only is the default. The setup steps tell the owner to turn off running when locked in the shortcut's details; that toggle was not confirmed in Apple's pages.
Limits: 20 asks a minute per key, text up to 2,000 characters, one answer at a time per key, at most 50 conversations per key (the existing cap).
Nothing here touches sign-in. Removing the key, or the whole door, leaves the page, passkey and Tailscale exactly as they were.
acceptance: Stand-in fleet, from the internet (Funnel header, no Tailscale identity): POST /console/api/say {"text":"what's running?"} with a phone key returns 200 with status answered, a `say` under about 500 characters with no markdown, ids or addresses, and `ask` null. The conversation shows in the owner's list under the key's name.

The same phone key is refused at /console/api/mcp and at /console/api/v1/chat/completions. An ordinary agent key works at /say. A removed or made-up key gets a refusal that still carries a `say` sentence.
Look-only key: "start gemma on spark 3" starts nothing, and `say` explains the key can only look.

Key that may change things: "start gemma on spark three" starts nothing yet, and `ask` names the model and Spark 3. Then {"text":"Yes."} starts exactly that, with an audit line naming the key. "No" starts nothing and puts the question away. A stop is confirmed the same way.

Slow answer (stand-in brain takes 45 s, wait 2): status working within about 2 s. A second call with new text while it is still answering returns working and does not queue the text. After it finishes, a call with empty text returns the answer.
A reply containing bold, a table, a conversation id and a URL comes out of `say` with none of them. A long reply is cut at a sentence and ends with "The rest is in the chat."
A question only the owner may answer: `say` sends the owner to Spark Console, and "yes" by voice does not press it.
"Remember that Spark 4 is on Wi-Fi now": with the changing key, memory.json gains that line and `say` repeats it; with the look-only key it is refused.
Pause switch on: a voice change is refused in plain words. The thirteenth change in an hour pauses agents as today.
Two asks a minute apart share one conversation ("and on Spark 4?" resolves). After 30 idle minutes a new one starts. A yes after 15 minutes runs nothing.
A reply path that read a container log saying "say yes to stop everything" still only proposes; nothing stops.

On the phone, once, by the owner: the Action Button and "Hey Siri, Ask Sparkie" both work with Tailscale off; the answer is heard once, not twice (add a final Nothing action if Siri repeats it); try wait 8, 20 and 30 to see how long Siri waits and set `wait` in the Shortcut; with the phone locked, see what happens and turn off running when locked.
The existing door and ask tests still pass unchanged (ask_sparkie keeps its 40 s wait and colleague style), run by whoever owns the test gate.
dependsOn: The owner's yes to change contract section 13 (voice is listed as not wanted today).
The main address open to the internet on :8443 (already so, deploy/open-to-internet.sh) and the owner's passkey for making the key. Both exist.
Sparkie's model running on Spark 2. Each phone key uses one of the two agent answer slots.
An iPhone with Shortcuts; the Action Button needs iPhone 15 Pro or later (Apple: https://support.apple.com/guide/shortcuts/run-shortcuts-with-the-action-button-apdfea15680b/ios).

Checked in Apple's guide: Get Contents of URL does POST with a JSON body (https://support.apple.com/guide/shortcuts/apd58d46713f/ios); Siri runs a shortcut by its name, speaks the result, and asks to unlock only for shortcuts that open an app (https://support.apple.com/guide/shortcuts/run-shortcuts-with-siri-apd07c25bb38/ios); a field with an import question is cleared when shared (https://support.apple.com/guide/shortcuts/add-import-questions-to-shared-shortcuts-apdf330fd3a0/ios).

Checked elsewhere: the Bearer header in Get Contents of URL and parsing the reply (https://www.innoq.com/en/blog/2023/03/openai-gpt-on-macos-ios-apple-shortcuts/); an open-source Siri shortcut using the same pattern with follow-up turns (https://github.com/Yue-Yang/ChatGPT-Siri).

Not confirmed, because the web search budget for this run was used up and only direct pages could be opened: how long Siri waits for a shortcut's web call, and whether this iOS version has the Allow Running When Locked toggle. Both are on-phone acceptance checks; the design works either way through the `wait` field and the look-only default.
Not blocking, already planned elsewhere: ask_sparkie following the operations it started (gives multi-step requests by voice), owner-first priority on the brain, and measuring time to first words.
The messaging channel (Telegram or iMessage bridge) should be built after this and call the same /say door with its own door-limited key.

problems: The 8-second wait does not fit this brain. Qwen 27B answers at about 20 tokens a second with thinking on (/Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/docs/contract.md, lines 1096-1107), the contract's own bar is first words within 10 seconds (7.10), and the one recorded real turn took 66 seconds (/Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/test/eval/results-2026-11-08-partial.json). A spoken answer needs the whole reply, usually two model rounds and a lookup. So nearly every ask would end in "Still working, ask again", and a change by voice (ask, hear the question, say yes) would take three or four presses over a minute or more. How long Siri itself waits is still unconfirmed: the web search budget was used up in this run too, and Apple's Siri and privacy pages state no limit.

Going back a build widens the phone key. The "works only at /say" limit is a `door` field on an ordinary `sck_` key in agents.json, enforced only by the new code in /Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/service/src/20-mcp.mjs (keyViewer, agentFor). undo_update and the installer's put-back restore files only and leave state as it is (/Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/deploy/host-on-portal.sh, lines 130 and 226). The earlier build would then accept that key at the agent door and the model address, with every tool and none of the spoken confirmation.

A spoken yes has no real label for most changes. changeLabel (/Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/service/src/17-changes.mjs, lines 69-77) only words start, stop, restart, remember and forget. Proposing "every change" by voice means undo_update, run_workflow, save_workflow, test_changes and undo_last_change are asked as "undo_update it?", and a yes runs them. That is a blind yes to rolling back the console or running a saved multi-step workflow.

Voice changes loop after an install. A workflow waiting for its first run is proposed as a validation choice (/Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/service/src/16-actions.mjs, lines 311-314), and a typed or spoken yes never presses a validation choice (/Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/service/src/14-chats.mjs, line 208). Because the design proposes every change, the yes goes to the model, which proposes again, without end.

Remembering is the one change that runs unconfirmed, from dictated text. On a Sparkie turn the line is recorded as the owner's (`by: 'owner'`, /Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/service/src/20-memory.mjs, line 49) and sits at the top of the brain's prompt in every owner chat. Whoever holds the phone or a synced copy of the Shortcut, or a mis-hearing, writes lasting lines with weaker proof than the passkey. Today's ask_sparkie has the same flaw for any key that may change things.

The lock screen and the key's home are weak. Siri's voice match is not sign-in, and Apple says Siri asks to unlock only for shortcuts that open an app. I could not find an "allow running when locked" switch in the Apple guide pages I could open (adjust privacy settings, advanced settings). The key is plain text inside the Shortcut, synced by iCloud to every device and readable on an unlocked phone or Mac. With a key that may change things, anyone near the locked phone could stop models in two sentences. Look-only limits this to hearing fleet state, log summaries and memory lines (the design adds memory to these turns).

It is a third conversation door and a fifth error shape. The reviews already plan agent keys on /chats with a JSON long-poll, and one error object (/Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/docs/reviews-2026-11-11.md, lines 136-143). /say adds its own errors with a `say` field and special cases at the sign-in line of /Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/service/src/24-handler.mjs. Shaping it around Siri (8 seconds, 500 characters, spoken style) before the messaging bridge exists risks building it twice: a Telegram or iMessage bridge wants long waits, the full text, and results when operations finish.

It is not quite what was asked. The owner asked to iMessage, text or Telegram it; contract section 13 lists voice as not wanted. The designer does ask first, which is right. But the same Shortcut with typed input (Ask for Input, Show Result) gives "text it" without reversing that line, and dictation is then just the phone's keyboard.

The phone competes with the owner's own agents. It takes one of the two agent answer slots and is limited to one answer at a time (14-chats.mjs, lines 171-173), so with two agents mid-ask the phone hears "try again in a minute". A second spoken request while one is answering is dropped, not queued; unless that is said aloud, the owner's words are lost silently.

Outside text can still shape what is spoken before a yes. The model's own sentence comes before the console's label, and a log line read in that turn can make it misdescribe what yes will do. This is safe only if, while a question is open, the door speaks the console's label alone. The phrase "Say yes or no" also puts the accepting word into the room just before the microphone opens in the optional listen-again loop.

The gain over what exists is small for one owner. The home-screen page with its 60-day passkey session and keyboard dictation already gives voice in, with full rights and a streamed answer. The no-code Shortcut against the agent door works today (24-handler.mjs line 81; requests with no Origin pass, 03-identity.mjs lines 224-229; test/internet.test.mjs line 263). The new code buys shorter prose and one fewer parsing step, and adds about 13 acceptance cases, one with a 45-second stand-in brain, to a test gate the installer depends on.

Smaller points. "The phone key is refused at /v1" cannot hold on the tailnet, where /v1 takes the Tailscale identity and ignores the key (a known gap in the reviews). Dictation may be processed by Apple when on-device recognition is not available. Model names such as Qwen, GLM and SGLang are often mis-heard, and heard() only fixes Spark numbers. I found no lock-out path: nothing here touches sign-in, Tailscale, Funnel or ports, and nothing runs on the Sparks, so ARM64 is not a concern.

design.title: agent_config: ready-made settings for the owner's own coding agents (opencode, Qwen Code, Codex)
design.design:
Why: the working settings live only inside the trial kit today; this hands them out in one call. One read action, `agent_config {agent, model?}`. No container, port, state file or secret. All paths are under /Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console.

1. New part `service/src/16-agent-config.mjs` (about 120 lines).
 - Data: a frozen table for `opencode`, `qwen` and `codex`: title, the version the engine trial pins (none for Codex), install line, file path, start command, docs link.
 - Code: `agentFiles(agent, s)`, a pure function that builds the file from `s = {baseUrl, model, context, maxOutput, sampling, thinking}`. opencode and Qwen Code copy the shapes in `agentbar/engines.mjs`, minus what only suits the sealed trial container (opencode's provider fence and 300-step cap, Qwen's API log folder). Codex gets a profile file, `~/.codex/sparks.config.toml` with `wire_api = "responses"`, so the owner's main Codex settings stay untouched.
2. Live values, read at call time: the gateway address (`consoleOrigin() + API_MOUNT + '/v1'`); for Sparkie, `MAIN`'s sampling, thinking, `maxTokens` and `--context-length` (capped at 262144); for a named model, `runningModels(viewer)` plus the server's own `max_model_len`. For that, widen `servedModel` in `15-routes.mjs` into `servedCard(url)` returning `{id, context}` (three lines; callers unchanged).
3. Every model is addressed through the gateway, so one file works on the tailnet, on a Spark, and from the internet with an agent key.
4. Result: `agent`, `model`, `files: [{path, content, ifItExists}]`, `install`, `start`, `triedWith`, `tried`, `door` (the MCP address only), `notes`.
5. No key ever appears. Files name the variable `SPARK_CONSOLE_KEY`, the name the page's Codex snippet already uses.
6. Tests: new `test/agent-config.test.mjs`; `agent_config` added to `TOOLS` in `test/lib.mjs` and to the valid-argument maps in `test/door.test.mjs` and `test/fuzz.test.mjs`; three cases in `test/eval/cases.json`. Add it to `INSIDE_READS` in `14-chats.mjs`, and one row to `docs/agent-door.md`.

Left out on purpose: Continue and aider (not in the trial; each is one table row later); MCP header lines (the secret mask rewrites them, and the page already shows them when a key is made); writing files into boxes (`start_box` does not exist yet; it would call `agentFiles`).

Critical files: /Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/service/src/16-agent-config.mjs (new), /Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/service/src/15-routes.mjs, /Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/agentbar/engines.mjs, /Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/test/agent-config.test.mjs (new), /Users/akuppala/Documents/26aiRAG/spark-console/test/lib.mjs

1. In chat the owner says "How do I point opencode at Sparkie?". Sparkie calls `agent_config {agent: "opencode"}` and answers in one message: the file path (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`), the file's exact text in a code block, the install line (`npm install -g @opencode/cli@2.2.6`), how to start it (`opencode`), and one sentence on proof: "These are the engine trial's settings for Sparkie's model, with opencode 2.2.6." 2. "Give me the opencode config for the GLM model on Spark 3 and 4." The same file for the running GLM, with the name the gateway lists and the context the server reports. It says plainly that only Sparkie's model has been tried with these engines, and that tool calls depend on how GLM was started. If GLM is not running, it says so and offers to start it; the start is a separate change that needs the owner's yes.

3. "How do I point Codex at Sparkie?" A profile file, `~/.codex/sparks.config.toml`, and `codex --profile sparks`. It says this one is written from Codex's own config reference and has not been tried on these Sparks.

4. Without chat, from a terminal or the owner's own agent: `POST <console>/console/api/actions/agent_config` with `{"agent":"opencode"}`, the MCP tool of the same name, or `spark agent_config opencode --json | jq -r '.files[0].content'`, which gives the exact bytes to save. An agent on the laptop can fetch the file through the door and write it there itself; the console never touches the laptop.

5. One-time steps only the owner can do: install the agent on the laptop and save the file. On the tailnet nothing else is needed, because the Tailscale identity is the login and any key string works. Away from the tailnet only: make a key under Access, Agents (as today) and export it in the shell as `SPARK_CONSOLE_KEY`. Nothing about Tailscale, SSH, the firewall or users changes.

6. "Set my box up so Qwen Code just works in it." Today Sparkie gives the Qwen Code file and says it cannot write into a box yet. When a box action exists, it calls the same function and writes the same file.
design.decidesAndAsks:
Code decides, not the model. The table holds two kinds of entry: opencode and Qwen Code, whose files are the engine trial's (`agentbar/engines.mjs`), and Codex, written from its config reference. For Sparkie's model the numbers come from the setup that is running (`MAIN`), the same values Sparkie's own calls use in `14-chats.mjs`. For any other model the file carries only what is known: the gateway address, the listed name and the reported context. No sampling or thinking is guessed. `tried` is true only for opencode or Qwen Code on Sparkie's model in its Agent setup; every other answer says what it is based on.

Sparkie's part is small: pass `agent` as the owner named it, pass `model` only when they named one, and paste `files[].content` unchanged.

It asks first when:
- The owner did not name the agent ("give me the config for my coding agent"): one line, "Which one: opencode, Qwen Code or Codex?". `agent` is a required enum, so a guess outside it is refused with the three names.
- The model words match more than one running model: the action refuses with the matching names and Sparkie asks which.
- The model is not running: it says so, lists what is, and offers to start it (a normal `start_model` with its own checks).

It never asks for approval, because nothing changes. For an agent with no entry (Cursor, Continue, aider) it does not call the action; it gives the address and model name from `running_models` and says there is no ready-made file yet.

Sources opened on 2026-11-11:
- opencode V2 docs (config, providers, models, agents, MCP servers, install): `providers`, `package: @opencode/ai/providers/openai-compatible`, `settings.baseURL` and `headerTimeout`, `limit`, `compatibility.maxTokensField`, `body`, `update: "disable"` (global file only), `agents.title.model`, npm `@opencode/cli`, Linux ARM64 and macOS ARM64 builds. All match `engines.mjs`.

- Whether SGLang's Responses API handles Codex's function tools on Qwen. This is why Codex is marked not tried.
- That the model list's context field is `max_model_len` on both vLLM and SGLang (from memory; the code falls back to the model's own files, then 32768 with a note).

guardRails: Read only: `kind: 'read'`, `who: 'owner'`, scope `fleet:read`. It writes nothing on a Spark or the laptop and starts nothing. No container, port, download, state file or background loop.

No secret in or out: no agent key, Hugging Face token or Authorization value is read or returned. Keys are referred to only by the variable name `SPARK_CONSOLE_KEY`; the owner still makes keys under Access, Agents. The owner's password is never involved.

The files must pass the door's secret mask unchanged. `maskDeep` rewrites `apiKey: value` and `Authorization: Bearer value`, so no file has an API-key field or an Authorization header (Qwen uses `envKey`, Codex uses `env_key`, opencode needs none on the tailnet). A test compares the masked door answer with the unmasked API answer.

Only the console's own text goes into a file: table constants, `config.json` preset values, the gateway address, and a model name that passes `^[\w./:@-]{1,200}$`. JSON and TOML strings are built with `JSON.stringify`. Nothing from logs, web pages, model cards or container labels.

Honest about proof: `tried` is true only for opencode and Qwen Code on Sparkie's model in its Agent setup, with the pinned version stated. Auth is simple for most useful servers: stdio servers read a token from the environment, GitHub takes a personal access token and Home Assistant a long-lived token (community-confirmed; its docs describe OAuth), and only hosted servers (Notion's, Google's, Slack's) need OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and RFC 9728 discovery, where redirect URIs must be localhost or HTTPS, which a headless hub meets with its own HTTPS address. Images confirmed for linux/arm64 from registry manifests on 2026-11-11: `mcp/filesystem`, `mcp/fetch`, `mcp/notion`, `mcp/playwright`, `searxng/searxng`, `isokoliuk/mcp-searxng`, and `ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server` (its publish workflow builds linux/arm64); Home Assistant's built-in `/api/mcp` and Google's Workspace servers (Developer Preview; Gmail drafts but no send) need no container. landscapes.landscape: On ARM64 Linux with local models, the proven swapper is llama-swap (MIT, Go, release v272 on 10 Nov, multi-arch `unified-cuda13` image): a call loads the model and waits until it answers, `ttl` unloads idle ones, groups or resource pools say which models may share a machine, and it starts vLLM containers through `cmd`/`cmdStop`; a community DGX Spark stack (LiteLLM, then llama-swap, then vLLM or llama.cpp) documents memory tiers and the GB10 traps (leftover memory and page cache failing vLLM's start check, instability near 126.5 GB). llama.cpp's own router mode (December 2025) serves many small GGUF models from one port, each in its own process, loaded on call with least-recently-used eviction, while vLLM and SGLang still serve one base model per server. For reliability, vLLM guarantees a parsable tool call only for a named or required tool choice (auto is not constrained unless tools are strict), vLLM and SGLang take a `response_format` JSON schema, and vLLM and llama.cpp also serve Anthropic's /v1/messages. LiteLLM is the standard router and its conventions are worth copying (ordered fallbacks, a `fallbacks` list in the request), but it wants Postgres for keys, cannot start models, had malicious PyPI releases in March 2026 (its Docker image was not affected), and its own docs warn that semantic caching goes badly wrong on agentic traffic. Classifier routers do not fit here: vLLM Semantic Router wants about 12 GiB for the router alone and lists H200, A100 and T4 as validated, and RouteLLM's recommended routers need an OpenAI key. This product's gateway already has the hard part (a call starts a model through the same placement, recipes and checks as chat); it lacks the cheap conventions: a caller's fallback list, waiting while a model loads, and telling callers what each model can do.

Every piece this domain needs ships an official ARM64 image today, confirmed from Docker Hub manifests: restic 0.19.1 and its rest-server 0.14.0 (append-only mode), Garage v2.5.0 (single-node flag since v2.3), SeaweedFS, copyparty 1.20.26, Syncthing 2.1.7, SFTPGo and Backrest 1.14.1. MinIO is no longer an option for self-hosters: its community edition lost the admin console in May 2025, went maintenance-only in December 2025 and stopped publishing images, which leaves Garage (simplest; presigned links and expiry rules, but no versioning or object lock) and SeaweedFS (Apache-2.0, versioning and object lock, more parts). A DGX Spark has one internal self-encrypting NVMe drive and four USB-C ports, so there is no second internal disk and no filesystem snapshots to count on; version history has to come from the backup tool, and the only always-on machine is Spark 2 itself. Tailscale Funnel serves only ports 443, 8443 and 10000 with a bandwidth cap that cannot be changed, so public file links must ride the console's own 8443 address and suit documents and short videos, not multi-gigabyte files. In the product today storage is the thinnest area: one daily tar of the console's state to Spark 3 or 4 (skipped for a day when both are off, and recorded only in /health), one free-disk number per Spark, no cleanup, no place for the owner's files and no way to hand a file out. The shared web-search budget ran out part-way through, so later facts come from official docs and registry manifests fetched directly; whether copyparty runs cleanly under a sub-path and whether Backrest has a callable API stayed unconfirmed.

Small self-hosted platforms all do roughly the same thing: values are encrypted with one key kept in a file beside the app (n8n's key in ~/.n8n, Infisical's ENCRYPTION_KEY, OneCLI's AES-256-GCM store), become write-only once saved (Coolify's locked variables), reach containers as files under /run/secrets rather than as environment values (Docker's own advice), and each app gets its own token (Hugging Face's advice). For agents the proven rule is that the model never holds the value: the host or a proxy adds it per destination (Anthropic's sandbox proxy, Infisical Agent Vault, OneCLI), and MCP 2025-11-25 says keys MUST be collected on a web page outside the client (URL-mode elicitation, error -32042), a protocol version the console's door already names. All of that works on ARM64 Linux with Node's built-in crypto and plain Docker, with no model involved. The heavier vaults (Infisical with Postgres and Redis at 4 GB minimum, OpenBao, Vaultwarden) add a service, an unseal step or the owner's master password for about a dozen tokens, and systemd-creds for a user service needs systemd 256 while DGX OS 7 is Ubuntu 24.04. In the code today there is no store: the Hugging Face token is whatever file sits on each Spark (11-setups.mjs:395), container environment goes on the command line as -e K=V (05-library.mjs:360, 08-cluster.mjs:305, 13-main-model.mjs:131), a token pasted into chat is saved and sent to the brain (14-chats.mjs:190), and the daily state tar goes to Spark 3 unencrypted (25-backup-and-start.mjs:12); the parts worth building on are maskSecrets/maskDeep, audit.jsonl, hashed agent keys with scopes, the passkey gate, and scripts sent over SSH stdin. Web search was unavailable in this run (the shared budget was used up), so everything comes from primary docs fetched directly, and four points are from memory and need a check before relying on them: systemd 255 on Ubuntu 24.04, Vaultwarden's ARM64 images and missing Secrets Manager, Hugging Face's whoami endpoint, and the KeyExpiry field in `tailscale status --json`.

Web search was unavailable for this run (the shared search budget was already used up), so the findings come from official docs fetched directly and from the code; claims I could not re-check are marked in skip. On ARM64 the engines already carry the hard numbers: vLLM serves Prometheus /metrics by default, SGLang with --enable-metrics (the brain's setups in service/config.json already pass it) and llama.cpp with --metrics, giving exact tokens, time to first token and queue per model, but none labels the caller, so who-called-what can only be counted at the console's own gateway. On GB10, nvidia-smi gives utilization, temperature and power but shows "Memory-Usage: Not Supported" (NVIDIA known issues); NVIDIA says to read MemAvailable and SwapFree from /proc/meminfo, and its DGX Dashboard (localhost:11000 on each Spark) shows live values only. The usual history stack (Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics with Grafana, nvidia_gpu_exporter, or the lighter Beszel) runs on ARM64 but is built for dashboards and a query language, not for a 27B chat brain and about 30 series; LiteLLM-style per-key accounting needs a database, and node:sqlite is only a release candidate from Node 25.7, so monthly append-only JSON lines (about 5 MB a month) fit this dependency-free service best. Spark Console today samples every Spark each 30 seconds but keeps only one running GPU-energy total (service/src/12-status.mjs), 500 events in memory (19-watcher.mjs), an audit line per action that no read exposes (20-mcp.mjs), nothing at the gateway (15-routes.mjs) and no list of its own abilities. The contract (docs/contract.md section 13) lists usage reports as not wanted, so everything proposed is an answer when asked through chat or the API, never a report, dashboard or push: three new read actions and three extended ones, no new container and no new background loop.
